title: Section 73: the power and its two hard limits
paras: So let's start with section 73 — the power itself, and the two hard limits built into it. What section 73 lets you do, in the words of the statute, is apply "for planning permission for the development of land without complying with conditions subject to which a previous planning permission was granted". And on that application, the authority looks at one thing only: the conditions subject to which permission should be granted — that's section 73, subsection 2. It can grant subject to different conditions, subject to none at all, or it can refuse, if it takes the view the original conditions should stand. What it isn't is a chance to reopen the principle of development. But — and watch this — the authority must have regard to the development plan and material considerations as they stand at the date of the section 73 decision, and those may well have shifted since the original grant.

There are two statutory limits sitting inside the section. The first is simple enough: it's confined to conditions. It assumes you've already got a permission carrying a condition to vary or remove, so you can't use it where there's no relevant condition to alter. The second one people forget all the time. It's section 73, subsection 5, and it prohibits a grant that has effect to change a condition by extending the time within which development must be started, or reserved matters applied for. In other words, section 73 cannot extend the life of a permission. That old habit of "renewing" a permission by varying its commencement condition? That died the day section 73, subsection 5 took effect.

Now, here's the thing about a section 73 grant — it doesn't amend the original permission. It creates a new, free-standing permission that sits alongside the original, and the original stays extant unless and until it lapses. The developer gets to pick which one to implement. And that duality cuts two ways. Where the original's been partly built, the section 73 permission — remember, that's a permission for the whole development as varied — has to be capable of coherent implementation across the whole site. And where two permissions subsist over the same land, the Pilkington principle, which we'll come to in topics five and six, decides whether implementing one shuts the door on the other.

One thing that stirs up argument is timing. You can certainly make a section 73 application while the original permission is still extant. Whether you can make one after the original's time limit for implementation has expired — that's far less settled. The orthodox and prudent view is that section 73 works on a subsisting permission, so get the application in before the original lapses. Don't assume an expired permission can be brought back to life by section 73.

title: The description limit: Finney and Armstrong
paras: Next, the description limit — and the two cases that draw the line, Finney and Armstrong. The single most important constraint on section 73 is this: it cannot alter the description of the development in the operative part of the permission. That's the ratio of Finney against the Welsh Ministers, reported at 2019, E-W-C-A Civ 1868. The permission described two wind turbines with a tip height "up to 100 metres". Along comes a section 73 application trying to lift the permitted height to 125 metres by varying the relevant condition. And the Court of Appeal — Lord Justice Lewison — held the grant unlawful. Section 73, subsection 2 confines the exercise to the conditions; it gives no power to change the description of the development for which permission was originally granted. So if the description has to change, section 73 is the wrong tool. What you need is a fresh application — or section 73B, once it's in force.

Section 73 gets called the route for a "minor material amendment", but be careful — that label describes common practice, not a legal limit. Armstrong against the Secretary of State, reported at 2023, E-W-H-C 176, Admin, confirmed there's no statutory ceiling in section 73 on the extent of change. The claimant held permission for a single dwelling and applied to vary the approved-plans condition to alter the building's architectural design. The authority refused, and then an inspector refused — both on the footing that the changes were too material for section 73. And the High Court said they'd misdirected themselves. The materiality of the changes was simply irrelevant to whether the power was available, provided the description of development — "a single dwelling" — stayed unchanged, and the varied conditions stayed consistent with it.

Read the two together and you've got one axis of the modern boundary fixed. It isn't the size of the change that matters — it's consistency with the operative description. Even fundamental changes to an approved scheme can be made by section 73, so long as you don't contradict the words describing the development in the operative part. And that's exactly why the drafting of the original description, years before, quietly sets the ceiling on how much flexibility a scheme will ever have.

The practical upshot runs upstream, to every new application you touch. A tightly drawn description — "erection of 14 dwellings in accordance with the approved plans" — is a straitjacket. A loose one — "residential development" — leaves you room to vary conditions substantially down the line, without a fresh application. So the description isn't boilerplate. It's the width of the door every future amendment has to fit through.

title: Fiske and Lambeth: conditions cannot negate or omit the grant
paras: Now to Fiske and Lambeth — and the rule that conditions can't negate the grant, or quietly drop out of it. If Finney stops you changing the description head-on, Test Valley Borough Council against Fiske, reported at 2024, E-W-C-A Civ 1541, closes off the obvious workaround: you can't achieve by condition what you can't achieve to the description. The original permission was for a solar farm with a substation. The operative part referred to a substation, the approved plans showed a 33 kilovolt substation, and condition 15 required its details. Then a section 73 permission kept the word "substation" in the description, but pulled it out of the approved plans and deleted condition 15. And the challenge succeeded. Lord Justice Holgate held that a planning permission is made up of the operative part and its conditions, and it's unlawful for a condition to "derogate from or negate" the operative grant. The operative part can't give consent with one hand and let a condition take it away with the other. A section 73 permission that's internally inconsistent with its own operative part is bad.

Fiske also nailed down the corollary that's decisive for phased schemes: a condition on one permission can't lawfully modify a separate permission. The two grants are legally distinct, and one can't reach across and amend the other. That principle comes back in topic six, on drop-in permissions.

How you read a section 73 permission — especially where the notice leaves a condition out — got settled by R, on the application of Lambeth, against the Secretary of State, reported at 2019, U-K-S-C 33. Lambeth granted a section 73 permission varying a condition on a retail unit but, through a drafting error, failed to re-impose the condition restricting use to non-food goods. And the Supreme Court held the use hadn't thereby become unrestricted. Construing the permission as a whole, through the reasonable reader who knows the planning history, "the limited description of the use must be read as if it were itself a condition" — those are Lord Carnwath's words. The restriction survived the omission.

This one's easy to state backwards, so let me state it carefully. Lambeth is not authority that an omitted condition falls away — the Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeal on exactly that point. It's authority that a section 73 permission is construed in full context, so a restriction can go on binding even if it isn't restated. Which means the safe practitioner course hasn't changed. Re-state, in terms, every condition you intend to continue, and rely on neither the presence nor the absence of a condition to change the substance. A consolidated decision notice — the full description, the entire set of conditions as varied — is the discipline that makes the permission readable, and implementable, as one document.

title: Section 73A: permission for what is already built
paras: Section 73A next — permission for what's already built. Section 73A is a separate power, and it gets confused with section 73 constantly because of the numbering, but it does something quite different: it authorises planning permission for development already carried out. Under section 73A, subsection 2, permission can be granted in three situations. First, for development carried out without permission. Second, for development carried out without complying with a condition. And third, for development carried out before the expiry of a time-limited permission, where you're after retention beyond that period. A section 73A permission can be expressed to take effect from a date earlier than the grant — including the date the development was carried out — and that's what makes it genuinely retrospective, rather than a fresh prospective consent. It's the statutory basis of the "retrospective planning application".

These applications tend to come up in two ways. First, the landowner volunteering to regularise development already built — a barn conversion finished otherwise than in accordance with approved plans, say, or an unauthorised change of use. And second, the landowner reacting to the threat, or the service, of enforcement. The two routes to authorising past development overlap: you can often reach the same result through the ground A deemed application on an appeal against an enforcement notice under section 174, which invites the Secretary of State to grant permission for the development as carried out. So the tactical choice between a proactive section 73A application and leaning on a ground A appeal comes down to cost, timing, and the client's appetite for risk.

Two points of professional caution here. Making a section 73A application isn't, in law, an admission that permission was required — but in practice it's often treated as an acceptance that the development is unauthorised, so don't make it reflexively. And section 73A won't cure a permission that was never lawfully implemented. It grants a new permission for what's been done, the merits get assessed afresh, and the authority is perfectly entitled to refuse — which leaves the development liable to enforcement.

That merits-afresh point is the one clients struggle with most. Retrospective doesn't mean forgiven. The authority weighs the development as if it were newly proposed, and the fact that it's already standing there earns it no planning credit. A scheme that would've been refused prospectively will be refused retrospectively — and the money already spent building it forms no part of the balance.

title: Phased schemes: the whole-scheme problem
paras: Now, phased schemes — and the whole-scheme problem. Large developments are hardly ever built exactly as first permitted. Markets move, a phase gets re-planned, a house type is swapped out, an access shifts. And the instinctive tool is section 73: vary a condition and press on. For a single-permission phased or masterplan scheme, that instinct is now dangerous — because two independent lines of authority converge to hem it in. The first is the Finney and Fiske limit on section 73 itself. The second, and more fundamental, is the Pilkington and Hillside rule that a permission for a multi-unit development is normally a single, indivisible whole. So a change to one part is, in law, a change to the entire permission.

The foundation is Pilkington against the Secretary of State, reported at 1973, 1 W-L-R 1527. Where two permissions subsist over the same land, and it's physically impossible to carry out the development one of them authorises because of what's already been done under the other, the first can't lawfully be implemented or continued. The test is physical possibility on the ground, judged against what the earlier permission, read as a whole, actually authorised. Pilkington is why a developer can't sit on a portfolio of overlapping permissions and build a hybrid of the lot. Implement one, and you may extinguish the practical ability to build the others.

The second building block is Sage against the Secretary of State, reported at 2003, U-K-H-L 22, which established the holistic approach to construing a permission. A permission for a building or operation authorises the development as a whole — not as a string of independently lawful fragments. A developer can't pick and choose which parts of a permitted scheme to implement and treat the built parts as separately authorised. Sage supplies the conceptual foundation — and it was decisive in Hillside — that a masterplan permission is a single integrated grant, not a collection of standalone consents for each plot or phase.

Put the two propositions side by side and you can see the trap opening up. Because the permission is one whole — that's Sage — and because implementing an inconsistent later permission can make the original physically impossible to complete — that's Pilkington — the ordinary developer instinct, grab a separate consent for the troublesome phase and carry on with the rest, is precisely the move that can sterilise the original permission. The next topic is the modern authority that pulled these threads together.

title: Hillside, Dennis and drop-in permissions
paras: So to Hillside, Dennis, and drop-in permissions. The threads got pulled together by the Supreme Court in Hillside Parks Limited against Snowdonia National Park Authority, reported at 2022, U-K-S-C 30 — the decisive modern authority on amending large schemes. A 1967 permission authorised 401 dwellings on a 28-acre site, to a detailed master plan. And over the decades, a run of further permissions authorised departures from that master plan — until the original layout could no longer be built as approved. The Supreme Court held the 1967 permission could no longer be relied on, and it laid down propositions of general application. First, a multi-unit permission is normally construed as an integrated whole, not a bundle of severable permissions. Second, where later development makes it physically impossible to complete the original as approved, the original can't lawfully be continued — that's Pilkington affirmed. Third, the departure has to be material — a truly minor variation won't sterilise the original. And fourth, severability is possible, but it has to be express, on the terms of the particular permission — never presumed. F Lucas and Sons against Dorking U-D-C, reported in 1966 at 17 P-and-C-R 111, was left undisturbed.

Hillside also dealt with "drop-in" permissions — a separate permission for part of a larger site, standing in for a portion of the original scheme. It didn't impose any blanket prohibition. But it made clear that a drop-in doesn't amend the original permission, and that implementing it may, through Pilkington, defeat your ability to complete the rest. The suggested orthodox route to amend a large scheme is instead a section 73 application varying the whole permission — re-granting the entire development as amended — subject, always, to the Finney bar on changing the description.

The post-Hillside fallout got tested in R, on the application of Dennis, against the London Borough of Southwark, reported at 2024, E-W-H-C 57, Admin. The Aylesbury Estate regeneration had been consented by a phased outline permission. Facing the Hillside problem, the developer went for a section 96A non-material amendment to slot in the word "severable" — so a later drop-in for one phase wouldn't imperil the rest. And Mr Justice Holgate held it wouldn't work. Phasing on its own doesn't connote severability, and — in his words — "simply inserting the bare term 'severable' into a permission does not make it severable". He pointed out that if phasing equalled severability, the statutory implementation time limits would apply separately to each phase — so some phases could go time-expired, a result nobody intended. And converting the permission into a severable one was a material change, well beyond section 96A.

The lesson of Dennis is stark. Severability has to be engineered into a permission from the outset, by deliberate drafting — you can't readily retrofit it onto an existing phased consent. Drop-ins are still possible, but hazardous, and the risks come in three. First, a drop-in doesn't vary the original, which still needs completion as a whole. Second, once the drop-in is implemented, Pilkington and Hillside may leave the balance of the original physically incapable of lawful completion. And third, Fiske confirms that a condition on the original can't be used to authorise or accommodate the separate drop-in. So where you do pursue a drop-in, it should cover enough of the site to leave a coherent, implementable whole — and the planning assessment should address the combined development scenario, not the parcel on its own.

title: Choosing the route — and the coming s73B
paras: Finally, choosing the route — and the section 73B that's coming. It all follows from one pivotal question, asked first: does the change touch the description of development? If it does, section 73 is off the table — that's Finney — and your choice is a fresh application or, once it's in force, section 73B. If it doesn't, section 73 is available for changes of any magnitude — that's Armstrong — provided the result is internally consistent, and that's Fiske. Genuinely non-material changes go to section 96A — but not a change that inserts severability, or is otherwise material, and that's Dennis. Extending time for commencement or reserved matters is barred under section 73, subsection 5, so that needs a fresh application. And regularising development already built is section 73A — merits assessed afresh, overlapping with section 174 ground A.

For a phased or masterplan scheme specifically, a practitioner needing to change it has, in mid-2026, four realistic options. First, vary the whole permission by section 73 — the orthodox Hillside route — re-granting the whole scheme as amended. That only works where the description is unchanged, per Finney, and the result is consistent, per Fiske. Second, a fresh full permission for the whole site — where the description has to change, or the scheme has moved substantially — which sidesteps the Pilkington and Hillside trap by re-permitting the whole thing coherently. Third, engineer severability from the outset for new masterplans — after Dennis, that's the only reliable way to preserve flexibility. Or fourth, a carefully structured drop-in — viable in limited cases, with the safeguards we've covered, and a clear-eyed read of the Pilkington risk to the remainder.

Section 111 of the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023 inserts a new section 73B into the 1990 Act — and it's widely understood as the intended legislative answer to Hillside and Finney. It'll permit an application to vary an existing permission, including its description of development, provided the authority is satisfied the development as varied is "not substantially different" from what's already permitted. It's designed to occupy the ground between section 96A — the non-material route — and a fresh full application, giving large phased schemes a lawful means of material-but-modest amendment that section 73 simply can't deliver, because of Finney.

As at mid-2026, though, section 73B isn't yet in force. It's waiting on commencement regulations, and the supporting procedural, fee and consultation framework. Until it's commenced, the four options above stay the working toolkit, and the Hillside analysis has to be applied to every material change to a phased scheme. The uncertain frontier — and I'll flag it honestly — is the precise test for when a phased permission is severable. Hillside and Dennis establish that it's possible, and that it must be express — but not the drafting that reliably gets you there.
